chunks: String, file and API coding tasks. The question: Write code to:

These are small, classic coding warm-ups: reverse a string, check if a word reads the same backward (a palindrome), find one piece of text inside another, change specific lines in a file, and sketch the functions a driver should offer.
The algorithms are easy. The interviewer watches for awkward cases, like empty text, and for thinking about whoever will use your code.
Reversing a row of letter tiles is like two people starting at opposite ends of a bench, swapping seats, and walking toward the middle.
When they meet or cross, everything is swapped. Checking a palindrome uses the same two people, but they compare tiles instead of swapping.
"hardware" is 8 characters plus the terminator, 9 bytes. The two-pointer loop swaps outer pairs until the indices cross, which takes n/2 = 4 swaps.
String: a row of characters. In C it ends with a zero byte, so it takes one byte more than its visible length.
Two pointers: two position markers moving through the same data, here one from each end.
Substring search: finding where a short piece of text (the needle) appears inside a longer one (the haystack).
Regular expression: a compact pattern for matching text, such as "a line starting with VDD". API: the set of functions another programmer calls to use your code.
Reverse "abc". Put one marker on the first letter and one on the last. Swap 'a' and 'c' to get "cba". The markers move inward and meet at 'b', so we stop.
One swap was enough: the middle letter stays put. Now the edge case: for an empty string there is no last letter.
In C, "length minus 1" on a length of 0 wraps around to a huge number, so a good answer checks for empty input first. That is the whole idea.

"Reverse and palindrome are two-pointer loops: indices at both ends moving inward, swapping or comparing, O(n) time and O(1) space, with care for empty strings and, for palindromes, case and punctuation.
Substring search checks the needle at every offset, O(nm) worst case, and KMP makes it linear, though in real code I'd use the library.
File tasks stream line by line with a regex and write to a new file. For an API I'd define init, read and close, return codes, units and ownership."
Quick check. In C, how many bytes does the string literal "abc" occupy in memory?
